summary:
Syria is a country trans visitors should not enter. The Penal Code remains the operative framework after the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024: Article 520 criminalises "sexual acts against nature" and Article 517 criminalises public indecency, and both are applied to women as well as men. There is no legal gender recognition procedure, and LGBTI organisations cannot register.

The security position for trans people has deteriorated since December 2024. The Guardians of Equality Movement documented waves of violence against Syrian transgender women over the first two months of 2025, with non-state armed groups and security forces implicated across several cities, and circulated video footage from February 2025 showing authorities detaining trans women. Any state actor or armed group operating today can act against a trans visitor under the existing criminal provisions, and there is no complaints mechanism or protective machinery that a foreign trans person could use.

Documented patterns of digital targeting persist: entrapment through dating and social applications and extortion of alleged homosexuality have been recorded throughout the conflict period, and a visitor using those channels in Syria carries the same exposure.

Nothing in the sources indicates screening, detention or placement rules specific to trans detainees, visa treatment of trans applicants, or access to gender-affirming care. Absence of those findings is not evidence of safety; the sourced picture is criminalisation without remedy alongside active trans-targeted violence.
tangentialFactors:
The violence recorded since December 2024 is not solely a state phenomenon. The Guardians of Equality Movement's April 2025 field investigation also worked to correct reporting that LGBTQIA+ individuals were being hunted in Homs, finding through its on-the-ground reporter network that the claim was inaccurate, an effort aimed at preventing incitement against the community. Verified and unverified claims circulate together in this environment, and a visitor cannot rely on public reporting to establish where threat is concentrated.

Lethal non-state violence has an extended record. Human Rights Watch's "Audacity in Adversity" tallied at least 16 killings in Syria claimed by ISIS for alleged sodomy as of June 2016, alongside 23 in Iraq and 3 in Libya, with activists including these cases in representations to the UN Security Council.

State enforcement predates the current transition. In June 2010 Syrian authorities raided a series of private parties over preceding weeks, arresting more than 25 men in the latest operation, most charged with homosexual acts and others with drug offences.

International attention has not translated into protection on the ground. In 2015 two gay refugees from Syria and Iraq addressed the first UN Security Council session dedicated to LGBT rights, a closed session co-sponsored by the United States and Chile, describing exposure to violence under authoritarian governments, militant groups and ISIS.
localsOnly:
Syrian residents live under Penal Code Articles 520 and 517, and the restrictions apply to women as well as men. Legal gender recognition is impossible, so identity documents cannot be aligned with a person's gender.

Everyday concealment remains the norm. Reporting from Damascus in October 2020 described homosexuality and public decency offences as illegal in the capital and a 36-year-old resident explaining that she meets friends in gay-friendly cafes only "in whispers".

LGBTI organisations cannot register, which removes the formal channel through which residents could seek protection or challenge charges.

Residents face the post-December-2024 wave of violence documented by the Guardians of Equality Movement, involving both armed groups and security forces, and continue to encounter entrapment and extortion through online applications. Syrians who fled have raised these conditions at the UN Security Council, with no reported change to the domestic legal position.
outOfScopeNotes:
The European UNHCR-affiliated EUAA country focus entry on treatment by state, non-state and societal actors recorded no usable finding for Syria in this inventory, so its assessment of actor behaviour remains unexamined here.

Whether Articles 520 and 517 survive in amended form under post-2024 governance is unresolved in these sources; the most recent country overview, updated 12 March 2026, still describes the Penal Code provisions as operative, but no legislative text from the transitional authorities was available to confirm amendment or repeal.

No sourced material covers entry or visa decisions affecting trans applicants, airport or border screening that could expose a visitor's gender history, detention classification by gender, or availability and legality of gender-affirming medical care.

The February 2025 detention footage and the reported arrests are described in monitoring reports without case outcomes, charges, or subsequent judicial proceedings, which remain unverified.
